name: Existentialism
era: From the 1840s, at its height in Paris from 1943 to 1960
line: You are free. Choose, and answer for what you choose.

quote.source: Existentialism Is a Humanism, lecture of 29 October 1945, published 1946, trans. Philip Mairet

quotes.text: Man is condemned to be free.
quotes.source: Existentialism Is a Humanism, 1946, trans. Philip Mairet

quotes.text: One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.
quotes.source: The Second Sex, 1949, opening of volume 2, trans. H. M. Parshley
The Myth of Sisyphus, 1942, last line, trans. Justin O’Brien

quotes.text: Anxiety is the dizziness of freedom.
quotes.source: The Concept of Anxiety, 1844, trans. Reidar Thomte
Garcin in the play No Exit, first performed in Paris in May 1944

quotes.text: In the midst of winter, I found there was, within me, an invincible summer.
quotes.source: Return to Tipasa, 1952, in the collection Summer

quotes.text: Life must be understood backwards. But it must be lived forwards.
quotes.source: Journals, 1843; a common English condensation of the entry

words.meaning: Being here, concretely, as this person
words.usage: What comes first. A human being turns up in the world and only afterwards defines what they are.

words.meaning: What a thing is; its nature
words.usage: A paper knife has one before it is made. A person, Sartre says, does not.
Not a possession. It is the very structure of being human: at every moment one must choose, and not choosing is a choice.
What freedom feels like from inside, when one sees that nothing forces or justifies the choice.
Kierkegaard’s word. Unlike fear it has no object. It is the awareness of possibility.
Lying to oneself to escape freedom, by pretending to be a fixed thing: I had no choice, that is just how I am.
Owning one’s freedom and one’s situation without excuses.
Camus’s term for the clash between the human demand for meaning and the silence of the world.
Camus’s answer to the absurd: to live fully and lucidly without appeal, and to refuse what degrades people.
Taking a side in one’s time. A writer who stays silent has also chosen.
Everything about me that is simply given: my body, my past, my birthplace, my death.
The human power to project past what is given towards what is not yet.
The gap that consciousness opens in being. Because I am not simply what I am, I can become otherwise.
The way things exist: solid, full, identical with themselves.
The way consciousness exists: always at a distance from itself, never finished.
The gaze of another person, under which I become an object and feel shame or pride.
Those through whom I come to know myself, and who can also fix me in a role.
Freedom is always freedom in a situation. Beauvoir stressed that some situations leave very little room.
The chosen direction of a life, towards which one throws oneself forward.
Being left without a God or a rulebook to tell us what to do.
Beauvoir’s word for the human condition: at once subject and object, free and bound.
In Sartre’s novel, the sick feeling that comes when ordinary things lose their names and are simply, stickily there.
Heidegger’s term for the kind of being that we are: the one for whom its own being is a question.
We did not choose to be born, or where, or when. We find ourselves already thrown into a world.
The faceless everybody whose opinions we adopt: one does this, one does not do that.
Living in the knowledge that one’s time is finite and one’s death is one’s own.
The basic structure of human existence for Heidegger: things matter to us.
Karl Jaspers’s term for death, suffering, guilt and struggle, where ordinary life breaks open.
Kierkegaard’s hero and addressee. He asked for these words on his gravestone.
The move into faith or commitment that no argument can make for you.

practices.name: I choose
practices.instructions: Write down the three main things you will do today. In front of each write the words I choose to. Not I have to, not I must. Then finish each sentence with because, and give your real reason. If you find you would not choose one of them, face that: either change it or choose it knowingly. Catch every have to during the day and rephrase it.
practices.why: Sartre held that we are condemned to be free: even under orders or in prison, we decide what to make of our situation. To say I have no choice is the commonest form of bad faith.
variations: Do it for the thing you most resent.
Say no to one thing you would normally drift into.
At a moment of indecision, note that not deciding is deciding.

practices.name: Describe the thing itself
practices.instructions: Go to a cafe with a notebook and sit where you can see. Order something and take your time. Choose one object in front of you, a cup, a glass, your own hand. For ten minutes describe exactly what you perceive, as if you had never seen such a thing: colour, edge, weight, how it is given to you. Leave out what you know about it. Then write for twenty minutes about anything, starting from there.
practices.why: The French existentialists began from phenomenology, the careful description of experience. Sartre’s conversion came around the turn of 1933 when a friend pointed at an apricot cocktail and told him that with this method he could make philosophy out of that glass.
variations: Describe a feeling in the same way, as it shows itself in the body.
Describe a person at another table without deciding who they are.
Work in the cafe for a whole morning, as they did.

practices.name: Catch your bad faith
practices.instructions: Look back over the last few hours for moments when you hid from your own freedom. There are two usual forms. In one you treat yourself as a thing: I am just a shy person, I am only doing my job, that is how I was raised. In the other you pretend you are pure freedom with no facts: my past does not count, I could stop any time. Write down one of each. Then restate both truthfully.
practices.why: Being and Nothingness describes a cafe waiter whose movements are a little too precise. He is playing at being a waiter, as if that were all he was. Bad faith is the wish to be a finished object and so be spared the trouble of choosing.
variations: Drop the phrase that is just who I am for a week.
Ask someone what excuse you use most.

practices.name: Commit to something
practices.instructions: Choose one thing in the world that you think is wrong and within your reach, however slightly. Do one concrete act about it today: write the letter, give the hour, join the group, tell the truth in the meeting, turn up. It must cost you something and it must be public enough that you can be held to it. Do not wait until you are certain.
practices.why: For Sartre and Beauvoir freedom that never acts is empty. They wrote, signed, marched and edited a journal for forty years, often wrongly, on the principle that to stand aside is also to take a position.
variations: Make a promise to another person and keep it.
Finish one thing you have been keeping open so as not to be judged on it.

practices.name: The rock and the summit
practices.instructions: Take the most repetitive task of your day, the dishes, the commute, the inbox, and do it tonight with full attention and no resentment, as the thing you are doing with this part of your one life. Then sit for five minutes with a plain fact: you will die, and you do not know when. Let it clarify. What, in the light of it, matters tomorrow, and what does not?
practices.why: Camus ends The Myth of Sisyphus with the man walking back down to his rock, conscious and unbowed: the struggle towards the heights is enough to fill a heart. Heidegger held that facing one’s own death is what frees a person from the They.
variations: Do the task badly on purpose once, then well, and feel the difference.
Write what you would regret not having done.
Watch the sun go down and name what was good today.

tasks.name: Listen to Miles Davis’s Ascenseur pour l’échafaud
Drink an apricot cocktail, or a coffee, and look at the glass
Journal: what did you choose today, and what did you let happen?
If nothing is laid down in advance, what do you owe?
Make one decision you have been putting off
Look one person in the eye and let them look back
Refuse one thing that everybody does

rules.why: Never say I have to. Own each act as yours, with your reason.
Not your nature, your parents, your job or the times. They are your situation, and what you do with it is yours.
Do not hide in keeping options open. Choose, and let yourself be judged by it.
Silence and neutrality are positions too. Commit where it matters, and say so.
Do not fix anyone in a role, and do not let them fix you. Will their freedom along with your own.
Let it sort the important from the trivial, daily.

read.title: Existentialism Is a Humanism
read.creator: Jean-Paul Sartre
read.why: The lecture that made the word famous. Clear, combative and short. He later thought it too simple, which is why it is the place to start.

read.title: The Myth of Sisyphus
read.creator: Albert Camus
read.why: Is life worth living if it has no meaning? An essay written at twenty-eight, in occupied France.

read.title: The Ethics of Ambiguity
read.creator: Simone de Beauvoir
read.why: The best account of what existentialist freedom asks of us in dealing with other people.

read.title: The Stranger
read.creator: Albert Camus
read.why: A clerk in Algiers kills a man on a beach and will not pretend to feelings he does not have. A hundred and twenty pages.

read.title: Nausea
read.creator: Jean-Paul Sartre
read.why: The diary of a man in a provincial town for whom the existence of things becomes unbearable, and then a kind of revelation.

read.title: At the Existentialist Café
read.creator: Sarah Bakewell
read.why: The whole movement told as a story of friendships and quarrels, with the philosophy made plain.

watch.title: Cléo from 5 to 7
watch.creator: Agnès Varda
watch.why: A singer wanders Paris for ninety minutes waiting for a medical result. A film about being looked at and beginning to look.

watch.title: Ikiru
watch.creator: Akira Kurosawa
watch.why: A Tokyo bureaucrat learns he has months to live and finally decides to do one real thing. Its title means to live.

watch.title: The Seventh Seal
watch.creator: Ingmar Bergman
watch.why: A knight home from the Crusades plays chess with Death to gain time for one meaningful act.

watch.title: Breathless
watch.creator: Jean-Luc Godard
watch.why: A small-time crook and an American student drift through Paris. The cinema’s version of a life improvised with no script.

listen.title: Ascenseur pour l’échafaud
listen.creator: Miles Davis
listen.why: Improvised in one night in Paris while the film played on a screen in the studio. The sound of the city after midnight.

listen.title: Songs of Juliette Gréco
listen.creator: Juliette Gréco
listen.why: The voice of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. Sartre wrote lyrics for her and said her voice held millions of poems.

listen.title: Le Déserteur
listen.creator: Boris Vian
listen.why: A polite letter to the president from a man who will not go to war. Banned from French radio for years.

listen.title: Existentialism
listen.creator: In Our Time, BBC Radio 4
listen.why: A forty-minute discussion of where it came from and what it claimed.

art.title: Walking Man I
art.creator: Alberto Giacometti
art.why: A thin bronze figure striding forward on heavy feet. Sartre wrote the catalogue essay for Giacometti’s first post-war show and saw in his figures the human being at a distance, alone and upright.

art.title: Photographs of Saint-Germain-des-Prés
art.creator: Robert Doisneau and Brassaï
art.why: The cafes, cellars and faces of the Left Bank as they were. Brassaï photographed Sartre and Beauvoir at the Flore.

art.title: Nighthawks
art.creator: Edward Hopper
art.why: Four people in a lit diner on a dark corner, together and separate. Painted in New York in the year of The Stranger.

art.title: Hostage series
art.creator: Jean Fautrier
art.why: Thick, scarred paintings of heads made while in hiding outside Paris, within earshot of executions.

eat.title: A hard-boiled egg at the counter
eat.creator: With salt, and bread
eat.why: The cheapest thing in a Paris cafe, taken from the wire stand on the bar. Writers lived on them.

eat.title: Croque-monsieur
eat.creator: Toasted ham and cheese
eat.why: Cafe food for someone who intends to stay at the table for six hours.

eat.title: Choucroute
eat.creator: Sauerkraut with sausages and pork
eat.why: The dish of the Brasserie Lipp across the boulevard, where they went when they had money.

eat.title: Couscous
eat.creator: Semolina with vegetables, chickpeas and broth
eat.why: The food of Camus’s Algiers, where he grew up poor in a working-class district.

drink.title: An apricot cocktail
drink.creator: Apricot liqueur with something stronger
drink.why: The speciality of the Bec-de-Gaz bar in Montparnasse, where Raymond Aron pointed at the glass and told Sartre and Beauvoir about phenomenology.

drink.title: Coffee
drink.creator: A small black one, made to last
drink.why: The price of a seat. During the Occupation they wrote at the Café de Flore all day because it had a stove.

customs.title: The cafe as a study
customs.creator: A table, a pen, the same seat
customs.why: Sartre and Beauvoir wrote in cafes from morning to night, at separate tables, and received visitors there.

customs.title: The review
customs.creator: Les Temps modernes
customs.why: Founded in 1945 to take a position on everything that happened. Its editorial meetings were held in Sartre’s flat.

customs.title: Signing
customs.creator: Petitions and manifestos
customs.why: They put their names to causes throughout their lives, among them the 1960 manifesto supporting the right to refuse to fight in Algeria.

customs.title: Refusing honours
customs.creator: No prizes, no institutions
customs.why: Sartre declined the Nobel Prize in 1964, saying a writer should not let himself be turned into an institution.

games.title: Football
games.creator: Team sport
games.why: Camus kept goal for a university team in Algiers until tuberculosis stopped him at seventeen. He said that what he knew most surely about morality and duty he owed to sport.

games.title: Chess
games.creator: Board game
games.why: The game the knight plays against Death in The Seventh Seal. Every move is a decision that cannot be taken back.

games.title: Boxing
games.creator: Sport
games.why: As a young teacher in Le Havre, Sartre boxed with his pupils. He was small, stubborn and enjoyed a fight.

festivals.title: Night of Ideas
festivals.creator: Late January, in Paris and many other cities
festivals.why: An evening and night of free public talks and debates organised each year by the Institut français.

festivals.title: Kierkegaard’s birthday
festivals.creator: 5 May
festivals.why: Born in Copenhagen in 1813. The city’s university and its research centre mark the day.

festivals.title: Simone de Beauvoir Prize
festivals.creator: 9 January, her birthday
festivals.why: Awarded in Paris each year since 2008 to a person or group defending the freedom of women.

places.title: Café de Flore
places.creator: 172 boulevard Saint-Germain, Paris, France
places.why: Where much of Being and Nothingness was written. Go early on a weekday, sit upstairs and stay a long time. The square outside is named for Sartre and Beauvoir.

places.title: Montparnasse Cemetery
places.creator: Paris, France
places.why: Sartre and Beauvoir share a plain pale stone just inside the main gate, usually covered in metro tickets and lipstick kisses.

places.title: Lourmarin
places.creator: Vaucluse, Provence, France
places.why: The village where Camus bought a house with his Nobel money. His grave in the cemetery is a rough stone with his name, among rosemary.

places.title: Tipasa
places.creator: Tipaza Province, Algeria
places.why: Roman ruins above the sea that Camus loved. A stele there carries his words about the right to love without measure. Check travel advice before going.

places.title: Assistens Cemetery
places.creator: Nørrebro, Copenhagen, Denmark
places.why: Kierkegaard lies in the family plot in what is now a much-used city park.

ethics.title: Responsibility
ethics.text: In choosing for myself I choose an image of what a human being should be. I am answerable for all of it.
ethics.practice: Take one decision today as if everyone would follow your example.

ethics.title: Authenticity
ethics.text: Live without self-deception about your freedom and your facts.
ethics.practice: Name one thing you do only because one does.

ethics.title: Willing the freedom of others
ethics.text: My freedom depends on theirs. To oppress is to contradict oneself.
ethics.practice: Give someone a real choice today where you would usually decide for them.

ethics.title: Lucidity
ethics.text: Look at what is the case, death and absurdity included, and do not flinch into comfort.
ethics.practice: State one hard fact about your life in a single plain sentence.

ethics.title: Solidarity
ethics.text: Camus: I revolt, therefore we are. Refusing injustice discovers a common ground.
ethics.practice: Stand beside someone today who is being treated as a thing.

ethics.title: Commitment
ethics.text: Values exist only where someone acts on them.
ethics.practice: Do one thing today that makes a belief of yours true.

philosophy.title: Existence precedes essence
philosophy.text: There is no human nature laid down beforehand. We exist first and define ourselves by what we do.
philosophy.practice: Finish the sentence I am, using only things you did this week.

philosophy.title: Condemned to be free
philosophy.text: We did not choose to be free, and we cannot resign from it. Even obedience is chosen.
philosophy.practice: Find one have to today and translate it into I choose to, because.

philosophy.title: Bad faith
philosophy.text: We flee freedom by pretending to be objects with fixed properties, or by ignoring the facts of our situation.
philosophy.practice: Catch yourself playing a part a little too well.

philosophy.title: The absurd
philosophy.text: We ask the world for meaning and it does not answer. Camus asks us neither to despair nor to invent a false answer.
philosophy.practice: Do one thing today simply because it is good to do, with no further purpose.

philosophy.title: The look
philosophy.text: Under another’s gaze I become an object. Relations with others are a struggle over who defines whom, and they can also be mutual recognition.
philosophy.practice: Notice when you feel watched, and how you change.

philosophy.title: Situation and ambiguity
philosophy.text: Freedom is never abstract. Poverty, sex, colour and history make the field in which each person chooses. Beauvoir insists we judge with that in view.
philosophy.practice: Whose freedom is narrower than yours today, and why?

philosophy.title: Being-towards-death
philosophy.text: My death is the one thing no one can do for me. Holding it in view pulls me out of the crowd and back to my own life.
philosophy.practice: If you had one year, what would you stop doing?

philosophy.title: The single individual
philosophy.text: Truth that matters has to be lived by someone. No system, crowd or church can exist in your place.
philosophy.practice: What do you believe that you have never acted on?

Where did you say I have to?

What rock do you push?

What did you refuse?

What will you choose tomorrow?

How has remembering death changed your days?
Whose freedom do you see more clearly?
What are you now willing to answer for?

intro: Existentialism is less a doctrine than a family of thinkers who start from the same place: the single human being, alive, free, mortal and obliged to decide how to live. Its ancestors are a Dane and a German of the nineteenth century. Søren Kierkegaard, writing in Copenhagen in the 1840s, argued against the great philosophical systems of his day that truth is something an individual must live, in anxiety and by a leap that no proof can make for him. Friedrich Nietzsche, a generation later, announced that God was dead and that we must create our own values. In the 1920s Martin Heidegger recast philosophy as the analysis of human existence: thrown into a world, absorbed in the anonymous They, and summoned to itself by the fact of death.

The movement that bears the name was made in Paris. Around the turn of 1933 a young teacher, Jean-Paul Sartre, was drinking with his companion Simone de Beauvoir and their friend Raymond Aron, who had been studying in Berlin. Aron pointed at his apricot cocktail and said that with the new German method one could talk about that glass and it would be philosophy. Sartre, by Beauvoir’s account, turned pale with excitement. He went to Berlin to learn it.

What he and Beauvoir built over the next fifteen years, in cafes because their rooms were unheated, was a philosophy of freedom. A human being has no fixed nature. We exist first and make ourselves by our choices. There is no God and no table of values to appeal to, so each of us is wholly responsible for what we become, and in choosing we propose a pattern for all humanity. The realisation is dizzying, and we commonly flee it by telling ourselves that we had no choice. Sartre called this bad faith.

These ideas came into their own under the German Occupation and after the Liberation, when questions of choice, collaboration and responsibility were matters of life and death. In October 1945 Sartre gave a public lecture so crowded that people fainted, and existentialism became a fashion, with its cafes, its jazz cellars and its black jumpers. Beauvoir applied it to the situation of women in The Second Sex, one of the most influential books of the century. Albert Camus, who refused the label, wrote in parallel about the absurd and about revolt. Maurice Merleau-Ponty explored the body, and Frantz Fanon the experience of the colonised.

The group broke apart over politics in the 1950s, above all over communism and the Algerian war. Structuralism replaced it in the universities. But its vocabulary of authenticity, commitment, anxiety and the absurd has never left ordinary speech, and its central demand has not dated.

This Onda asks you to live by that demand for a while: to speak of your acts as chosen, to describe what is in front of you, to catch your own excuses, to commit to something, and each evening to look at your rock and your death without flinching.
guide.origin: Copenhagen and Germany for its sources. Paris, on the Left Bank, for its great moment
guide.era: Kierkegaard wrote in the 1840s. The movement that took the name flourished from 1943 to about 1960

figures.name: Søren Kierkegaard
figures.bio: Danish writer who published under a crowd of pseudonyms, broke his engagement to the woman he loved, and attacked the comfortable Christianity of his country.

figures.name: Fyodor Dostoevsky
figures.bio: Russian novelist whose Underground Man and Ivan Karamazov set out the problems of freedom without God that later thinkers took up.

figures.name: Martin Heidegger
figures.bio: German philosopher whose Being and Time of 1927 gave the movement its concepts. He joined the Nazi Party in 1933 and never properly accounted for it.

figures.name: Karl Jaspers
figures.bio: Psychiatrist turned philosopher at Heidelberg. Dismissed by the Nazis because his wife was Jewish, he wrote after the war on German guilt.

figures.name: Gabriel Marcel
figures.bio: French Catholic philosopher and playwright who was among the first to use the word existentialism, and who gave it a religious form.

figures.name: Jean-Paul Sartre
figures.bio: Philosopher, novelist, playwright and tireless public figure. Short, wall-eyed, generous with money, and the most famous intellectual of his age.

figures.name: Simone de Beauvoir
figures.bio: Philosopher and novelist. Her partnership with Sartre lasted fifty-one years. The Second Sex and her memoirs made her a founder of modern feminism.

figures.name: Albert Camus
figures.bio: Born poor in French Algeria, he edited the Resistance newspaper Combat and won the Nobel Prize at forty-four. He died in a car crash three years later.

figures.name: Maurice Merleau-Ponty
figures.bio: The group’s most careful philosopher. He showed that we are in the world first of all as bodies.

figures.name: Frantz Fanon
figures.bio: Psychiatrist from Martinique who used existentialist ideas to describe the experience of racism and colonial rule, and joined the Algerian struggle.

history.detail: Either/Or and Fear and Trembling appear in Copenhagen under pseudonyms. They are little read outside Denmark for sixty years.
Dostoevsky’s narrator insists on his freedom to act against his own interest, simply to prove he is not a piano key.
Heidegger’s unfinished masterpiece is published and makes him famous at thirty-seven.
Aron tells Sartre and Beauvoir about phenomenology in a Montparnasse bar. Sartre spends the following year at the French Institute in Berlin.
Sartre’s first novel is published. He is a schoolteacher in Le Havre and then Paris.
Captured with his unit, Sartre spends nine months in a camp at Trier, where he reads Heidegger and writes a Christmas play.

history.what: The Stranger and The Myth of Sisyphus
history.detail: Camus publishes both in occupied Paris and joins the Resistance press.
Sartre’s major work appears, along with Beauvoir’s first novel, She Came to Stay.
Sartre speaks on whether existentialism is a humanism to an overflowing hall. The same month the first issue of Les Temps modernes appears.
Beauvoir’s two volumes sell twenty thousand copies in a week and are placed on the Vatican’s index of forbidden books.
After a harsh review of Camus’s The Rebel in Sartre’s journal, the two exchange public letters and never speak again.
Camus is killed in a crash in January 1960. Merleau-Ponty and Fanon die in 1961. Sartre declines the Nobel Prize in 1964.
Some fifty thousand people follow the coffin through Paris to Montparnasse. Beauvoir is buried beside him six years later.

concepts.detail: A manufactured object is conceived before it exists. A human being exists first, encounters themselves, and is afterwards only what they make of themselves.
Because nothing determines my choice, I am its sole author, and in choosing I affirm a value for everyone.
Anguish at the weight of choosing. Abandonment because no God or nature decides for us. Despair in the sense of counting only on what depends on our own will.
The attempt to escape freedom by identifying with a role or a nature, or to escape the facts by imagining oneself unbound.
Born of the encounter between human longing and the unreasonable silence of the world. It can be lived, with revolt, freedom and passion.
Other people reveal me to myself as an object in their world. Shame is the recognition that I am as they see me.
Each person is free within a concrete situation of body, class, sex, race and history. Beauvoir showed how a situation can be made into a destiny by others.
In Heidegger, resolutely taking over one’s own finite existence. In Sartre and Beauvoir, living one’s freedom lucidly and willing the freedom of all.
The passage from one way of life to another, aesthetic, ethical or religious, cannot be reasoned into. It is made, by the single individual, in fear and trembling.

facts.text: Sartre and Beauvoir placed first and second in the national philosophy examination of 1929. She was twenty-one, the youngest ever to pass.
They addressed each other with the formal vous all their lives.
Camus always denied being an existentialist, and Heidegger and Jaspers both rejected the label too.
Being and Nothingness weighed exactly a kilogram, and is said to have sold well in wartime to shopkeepers who used it as a weight.
Sartre wrote the screenplay for John Huston’s film about Freud. It ran to eight hundred pages, and he took his name off the result.
Kierkegaard walked the streets of Copenhagen daily, talking to anyone, and called it his people bath.

sources.title: The Ethics of Ambiguity
sources.creator: Simone de Beauvoir, trans. Bernard Frechtman

sensitivity.note: Existentialism asks you to look directly at freedom, death and the absence of ready-made meaning. This Onda treats those as sources of clarity. It is a philosophical exercise and is not meant to be done in a low state.
requiredCaveats: If thinking about death or meaninglessness weighs on you, stop the evening practice and talk to someone you trust or to a helpline.
Heidegger was a member of the Nazi Party. His concepts are used here because the movement cannot be explained without them, not as an endorsement of the man.
Sartre defended Soviet communism for years, and he and Beauvoir sometimes treated younger people in their circle badly. Admire the ideas with open eyes.
Radical freedom can sound like blaming people for their circumstances. Beauvoir’s point about situation is the corrective.
